articles.title: Smashing an Egg. That’s It, That's the Game
articles.summary: New Steam indie game Crack is all about smashing open a giant egg.
articles.body:
Is cracking a giant egg open the new Call of Duty? No, but Crack is further proof new Steam indie games are currently operating on a creative plane the rest of us can only hope to understand. It's a co-op game featuring an enormous egg in a laboratory. Nobody knows where it came from. Nobody knows what’s inside it. You've got a pickaxe and instructions to smash it open.

Things get more complicated from there. Crack promises an “incremental adventure,” meaning you don’t just stand around whacking the world’s largest omelette precursor with said pickaxe until something interesting happens.

You begin with relatively sensible egg-cracking equipment like pickaxes and chisels before progressing to dynamite and, apparently, “other weird tools” scattered around the mysterious laboratory. You can build scaffolding, and there are secret rooms, and any broken shells can be turned into currency. Most ominously, according to the press release for the game, "The egg has secrets," and, "The egg reacts to you. Whatever you do to it, it responds."

Honestly, it's a lot of pressure on whatever is inside that egg. Let's all take a moment to reflect on the sad tale of Peter Molyneux's Curiosity: What's Inside the Cube? Which promised the person that got to its core a life-changing prize. That prize turned out to be a revenue share in Molyneux's game Godus, which, at least by 2017, hadn't made a profit, and so there was zero revenue to share.

Crack is just the latest wonderfully specific game that Steam seems uniquely capable of promoting: Somebody has one deeply silly idea, refuses to dilute it with anything resembling good sense, and somehow ends up making the premise more compelling by taking it completely seriously. It feels like we're currently in a golden age for weird ways to burn time; there's a game called Needle In A Haystack Simulator where, well, you can figure out the main mechanic, and tidying up games are keeping people (and by people, I mean me) entranced by shelf stacking. Sadly, I've yet to find a game solely dedicated to peeling the labels off beer bottles in dive bars.

Crack will be released on Steam on October 26, and you can wishlist it here.

Rachel Weber is the Head of Editorial Development at IGN and an elder millennial. She's been a professional nerd since 2006 when she got her start on Official PlayStation Magazine in the UK, and has since worked for GamesIndustry.Biz, Rolling Stone and GamesRadar. She loves horror, horror movies, horror games, Red Dead Redemption 2, and her Love and Deepspace boyfriends.

articles.title: Xbox Elite Controller Series 3 Might Catch Up to Other Premium Controllers, According to Leak
articles.summary: It looks like Microsoft is getting ready to launch an updated version of the Xbox Elite Controller with some much-needed improvements.
articles.body:
The Xbox Elite Controller was my introduction to premium controllers, and while I still love the way it feels in my hand, it's simply fallen out of my rotation when I have access to controllers like the Steelseries Aeon Pro or the ROG Raikiri II. But, it looks like Microsoft is getting ready to launch an updated version with some much-needed improvements.

The leaks appeared on Reddit , based on configuration files found on Spectrum, the platform behind the Xbox Design Lab. Those files have since been taken down, but previously pointed to a controller that gives users the choice between Hall Effect and TMR (tunneling magnetoresistance) sticks, an audio scroll wheel and more paddle designs.

Xbox Elite Wireless Series 2 Controller Review

This isn't the first time the Xbox Elite Controller Series 3 has leaked. Back in August, a user posted pictures of a supposed prototype to Reddit . However, that leak didn't reveal much about how the controller worked, whereas this one purports to reveal the specs behind the rumored high-end controller.

With all of the supposed features in this latest leak, the new Xbox Elite Controller would go head-to-head with some of the best PC and Xbox controllers on the market, especially if it's a bit more durable. My current series 2 is in a state of disrepair where the thumbsticks don't click in anymore, and its missing an analog stick. The controller is also notorious for scattering into a dozen different pieces whenever you drop it, leading to the back paddles and the D-pad flying everywhere.

If Microsoft is able to keep the good parts of the Series 2, like its extremely long battery life and perfect weight, while also adding these leaked features, I could see the Elite Controller getting its crown back. At least, as long as it doesn't come with a higher price. After all, even a couple years after the Xbox Elite Series 2 launched, that controller will still set you back around $167 at the time of writing.

That price seemed worth it when the Series 2 first launched, but now that we have the $99 Steam Controller and the $129 Asus ROG Raikiri II , Microsoft has its work cut out for it in the high-end controller market.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra
